Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 1:

(p-١)In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Surat ash-Shu'ara' (The Poets)

Its purpose is that this Book is manifest in itself through its inimitability, which shows that it is from Allah, and it clarifies every ambiguity. Among this is another clarification of the surah before it, through its detailing and its descent upon the conditions of the nations and its portrayal of them. It also calms the grief of the Prophet (ﷺ), lest he fear that disbelief would engulf his community with humiliation, and that their enmity toward his followers would intensify into harm and aggression, as the word "sawfa" (soon) conveys of a long duration of time, by indicating the destruction of those known to persist in disobedience, and the mercy toward those whom He wills for guidance and goodness. Naming it "ash-Shu'ara'" is the strongest proof of this, by the way the Qur'an is distinguished from poetry through the loftiness of its station, the uprightness of its methods, the might of its aims, the truthfulness of its promise and its threat, and the justice of its good tidings and its warning. Likewise, naming it "ash-Dhulla" (the Cloud) indicates that it is more just (p-٢) in its exposition, or more indicative in all its affairs, than the measures indicated by the story of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) with the measure and the balance, and more burning than the cloud for whoever wars against Him in disobedience.

"In the name of Allah" (bismillah), who indicates the sublimity of His speech, the greatness of His affair and the might of His aims. "The Most Merciful" (ar-Rahman), who does not hasten against those who disobey Him. "The Especially Merciful" (ar-Rahim), who gives life to the hearts of those who love Him by granting success to what He is pleased with. ﴿Ta, Sin, Mim﴾ [perhaps this is an indication of the purity located at Dhu Tuwa, at the Mount Sinai (Tur Sina'), and Taba, Makkah, and the goodness of what was sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ), which combines all of that, as is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) what guides to this; and to the deliverance of the Children of Israel through what Musa (peace be upon him) heard of the eternal speech, and to the completion of their affair by preparing them for kingship through the drowning of Pharaoh and his armies and their victory over those who opposed them in that time, after their purification through long trials that brought them to the humiliation of servitude. All of this is an indication of a warning to Quraysh that, if they do not abandon their obstinacy, He will do to them what He did to Pharaoh and his armies of humiliation, in whatever manner He wills. He delivered His servants from them and made them mighty over everyone who opposed them].

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 2:

When He, glorified be He, distinguished in that (surah) between the true religion and the false creed, explained that distinction in the utmost clarity, separated the Most Merciful from the servants of Satan, and informed that He had made His Messenger ﷺ a message to all of creation, and concluded with a severe warning to the people who turn away [p. 3], after He had said: ﴿Then you have indeed denied (it)﴾ [Al-Furqan: 77]. At the time it was revealed, only a few of them had accepted Islam. This might give the impression that their destruction was near and that punishment would fall upon them, as was the case at the end of Surat Maryam. The disjointed letters (al-ahruf al-muqatta'ah) also pointed to something similar. This caused grief over the loss of what was hoped for, namely their mercy through faith and their protection from the calamities of events. It might also have led someone to suppose that their failure to accept Islam was due to a deficiency in the clarity of the exposition. God, glorified be He, removed that at the very beginning of this (surah) when He said: ﴿Those﴾, that is: the lofty verses of exalted purpose, which attain the highest degrees of perfection, composed of these letters with which you speak and the words of your tongue,

﴿are the verses of the Book﴾, that is: the one that gathers every criterion (furqan),

﴿clear﴾, that is: evident in itself that it is inimitable, that it is from God, and that it contains every sublime meaning, the one that distinguishes every confusing matter with the utmost clarity. Thus it is correct that, as was mentioned in the surah before it, clarification (al-ibanah) is separation and distinction. So the report that it is a criterion (furqan) came to frame the warning at the beginning and end of the preceding surah. And God is the Granter of success.

Imam Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: When Surat al-Furqan described the monstrous conduct of the stubborn disbelievers, and was concluded with what was mentioned of the threat, this was a likely occasion for his concern, peace and blessings be upon him, and his grief over the loss of their faith, because of the mercy and compassion with which he was created. So the next surah opened with consoling him, peace and blessings be upon him, and with (the fact) that had God willed, He would have sent down to them a sign that would overwhelm them and humble their tyrants. So He, glorified be He, said: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 3], and the two verses. This meaning recurs whenever consolation of him, peace and blessings be upon him, is intended, as in His, exalted be He, saying: ﴿Had God willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾ [Al-An'am: 35]; ﴿Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾ [Al-Sajdah: 13]; ﴿Had your Lord willed, all those on earth would have believed, all of them together﴾ [Yunus: 99]; ﴿Had God willed, they would not have done it﴾ [Al-An'am: 137]. Then God, glorified be He, followed this with admonition and reminder: ﴿Have they not seen the earth, how many noble kinds of every pair We have caused to grow in it?﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 7]; ﴿And when your Lord called Musa﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 10]. You rarely find in the Mighty Book the consolation of him, peace be upon him, occurring without being followed by the stories of Musa, peace be upon him, and what he endured from the Children of Israel and Pharaoh. In each story there is the acquisition of benefits, meanings and reports that the other does not acquire, so that no story is repeated, even if someone who does not reflect deeply supposes so. There is no story among the apparently repeated stories which, if it were dropped or assumed to be removed, would not lose a benefit that cannot be obtained from the others. This will be clarified in the tafsir, God willing. Then, exalted and high be He, followed the story of Musa with the stories of other prophets, peace be upon them, with their peoples, in the manner mentioned, and as companionship for him, peace and blessings be upon him, so that he would not destroy himself through grief over the loss of his people's faith. Then, glorified be He, followed that with mention of the Book and the great blessing of it, and said: ﴿And indeed it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 192]; ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 193]; ﴿upon your heart, that you may be among the warners﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 194]. How great is this honour, of which tongues fall short in thanking and minds are unable to measure. Then He, exalted be He, informed that it is ﴿in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 195]. Then He, glorified be He, informed of the exalted status of this Book and the widespread mention of it on the tongues of the messengers and prophets, saying: ﴿And indeed it is in the Scriptures of the former peoples﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 196]. He informed that the knowledge of the Children of Israel is among the greatest sign, the clearest proof and evidence, and that reflecting upon it is sufficient and its consideration is healing, so He said: ﴿Is it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 197], such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his like. Then exalted be He rebuked the hesitant Arabs, saying: ﴿And had We sent it down upon some of the non-Arabs﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 198], and the verse. Then He followed this with what the fearful believer takes admonition from: that the Book, although it is guidance and light, may be a trial for a group, as the Exalted said: ﴿He leads many astray by it and guides many by it﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 26]; ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease, it adds to their filth upon their filth﴾ [Al-Tawbah: 125]. Thus the Exalted said in this sense: ﴿Thus We have caused it to enter into the hearts of the criminals﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 200]; ﴿They will not believe in it until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 201], and the verses. Then the discourse returned to exalting the Book and magnifying it, that the devils should not scale over any part of it or reach it. So God, glorified be He, said: ﴿And the devils did not bring it down﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 210]; ﴿It is not fitting for them, nor are they able (to do so)﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 211], that is: they are not worthy of it, nor can they steal its hearing, but rather they are removed from hearing and pelted with shooting stars. Then God, exalted be He, enjoined His Prophet ﷺ, and the intended (audience) is the believers, and said: ﴿So do not call upon any other god along with God, lest you be among those punished﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 213]. Then He commanded him to warn and charged him with patience, saying: ﴿And warn your nearest kindred﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 214]; ﴿And lower your wing to those among the believers who follow you﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 215]. Then God, exalted be He, informed of the true target of what they imagined and the suitability of what they supposed, saying: ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 221]; ﴿They descend upon every lying sinner﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 222]. Then He described them, and all of this is an exoneration of His Prophet ﷺ from what they fabricated against him. Then He threatened and warned them, saying: ﴿And those who have wronged will soon know what overturning they will be overturned to﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 227]. End.

When he had already mentioned in that surah that he had been sent with his message to all creation, and had concluded with a warning against their denial of him in their staying away, together with the removal of all excuses, he negated every defect. This called for an intense grief on his part (ﷺ) over those who held back, as is the import of what comes next:

﴿Indeed, my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned.﴾ [al-Furqan: 30], as previously mentioned. That is because of the great compassion and profound mercy he (ﷺ) possessed. God the Exalted said, consoling him and removing his grief and comforting him, by way of resumption (istinaf, a new sentence that begins a fresh thought), pointing out that there is no deficiency in his warning, nor in the Book with which he warns, that could be a cause for their holding back from faith. The cause of that is purely the will of God the Exalted:

﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself﴾, i.e., destroying it through grief and killing it through sorrow, from bakha'a al-shah (he slaughtered the sheep), when he goes to the extreme in slaughtering it until he severs the bakhi' (a hidden vein in the spine and at the nape of the neck), with the letter ba' vowelled with a kasra, and that is the furthest limit for the slaughterer. [It] is different from the nukhā' (spinal cord), with the nun taking three vowels, since that is the white thread inside the vertebrae. ﴿That they not be﴾ i.e., so that they do not become, [i.e., a state as if it were their innate nature] ﴿believers﴾, i.e., firmly established in faith. It is as if it were said: this Book is at the utmost degree of clarity in itself and of making things clear to others. It has been mentioned in more than one place that upon you is only the delivery (of the message). Are you fearing and being apprehensive for yourself of destruction through grief and sorrow over their not having faith, while the situation is that, had We willed, We would have guided them, willingly or unwillingly? The apparent reading is that the clause of apprehension occupies the place of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to the demonstrative (the phrase "perhaps you would kill yourself"), just as the verse that follows it occupies the place of a circumstantial clause relative to it. That is, We indicate the verses that make clear Our purpose concerning them, while the situation is that you, because of your great eagerness for their benefit, are in a state in which one who does not know the unseen is apprehensive for you, lest you kill yourself with grief over their refusal to believe, while the situation is that, had We willed, We would have brought them that which overpowers them and humbles them into faith and other than it.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 4:

Since the one who loves is inclined toward what his beloved wills, He informed them that everything they are in is by His will, so He said: ﴿If We will﴾. He used the present tense here and in His words ﴿We send down﴾ to indicate the continuity of power. Since that sending down is by way of compulsion, dominion and subjugation (p-٨), He said: ﴿upon them﴾. And to confirm the intended meaning, He said: ﴿from the heaven﴾, i.e., the one in which We placed constellations (buruj) for benefits. He indicated the completeness of power by making it singular, so He said: ﴿a sign﴾, i.e., an overpowering one, as We did with some of those before them by uprooting the mountain and the like. He indicated the certainty of its effect by using the past tense in His words, coordinated with "nunazzil," because it carries the meaning of "anzalna": ﴿then their necks would remain﴾, i.e., immediately after the sending down, without delay, ﴿[bowed] to it﴾, meaning to the sign, always. But He expressed it with what conveys daytime, because it is the place of strength for all that is desired of turning, stratagems and resistance. ﴿Humbled﴾ is plural in this form because the verb belongs to its people, to indicate that their subjugation to it occurs while they are all together, and their gathering does not suffice, though it adds something. The original would be "fa-zallu" (then they would remain), but He mentioned the necks because they are the place of submission, for their suppleness appears after their rigidity and their bending after their haughtiness. And it points to the fact that submission happens naturally, without reflection, due to what overwhelmed and bewildered them of the greatness of the sign. So it is as if the act belongs to the necks, not to them. Khudu' (submission) means calmness, stillness and softness out of humiliation and subjugation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 5:

﴿Wa-mā﴾, i.e., this is Our attribute, and the situation is that there does not come to them, i.e., the disbelievers, ﴿any reminder﴾, i.e., any portion of admonition, remembrance and legislation that they would be reminded of (p-9), whereby it would be the cause of their remembrance and honour, ﴿from the Most Merciful﴾, i.e., the One whom they denied despite His blessings encompassing them, ﴿newly come﴾, i.e., in relation to its revelation and their knowledge of it. He indicated the persistence of their arrogance by His saying: ﴿except that they have been﴾, i.e., a state that is like their creation. By placing the prepositional phrase first, which indicates restriction, he pointed to the breadth of their thoughts and the strength of their resolve toward everything they turn to, and to the fact that their aversion from it has such strength that aversion from anything else is regarded as nonexistent alongside it. [So He said:] ﴿from it﴾, i.e., specifically, ﴿turning away﴾, i.e., an aversion that is a necessary attribute of theirs.

When the state of one who turns away from something is the state of one who denies it, He said: ﴿So indeed﴾, meaning: as a consequence of this action on their part, they have ﴿denied﴾, meaning: they have realized the denial and brought it near, as was mentioned at the end of that [passage], [and they mocked along with denying Our signs].

Since denying the threat is a cause of its being brought about, and since their denial of him (ﷺ) was in the state of one who mocks, for whoever denies something holds it in low regard and so becomes a target for ridicule, He said, threatening them: ﴿Then there will come to them﴾. He linked it by the particle fa' (fa', "then/so") and confirmed it with the letter sin (sin, the prefix marking the near future), and he reduced the delay mentioned at the end of al-Furqan (al-Furqan, the Criterion, surah 25) so that they would know that what they denied is certain to occur and that there is no place for denial in any way. ﴿News﴾, meaning: great tidings and consequences,

﴿of what﴾, meaning: the punishment which ﴿they used﴾, meaning: as a constant state, as if they had been created disposed to it, ﴿to mock﴾ at ﴿it﴾, meaning: specifically, because of their intense persistence in mocking it alone, ﴿they mocked﴾, meaning: they used to mock. (p-10) However, he expressed it with the verb form using sin to indicate that their state, in their intense desire for that mockery, is like the state of one who seeks it. [They have also added denial to it, so the verse is an instance of ihtibak (ihtibak, a rhetorical device in which something is omitted from two parallel parts, each part indicating the omitted counterpart of the other): he mentioned denial first as an indication of its omission second, and mockery second as an indication of the omission of its like first.]

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 7:

When their seeing of the heavenly and earthly signs, which necessitate submission and humility, necessitated the denial of their failure to heed what these signs call them to, let alone their mockery, and when the exhortation at the end of that passage to contemplate the constellations (buruj) of the sky and what follows from them of indications had preceded, the meaning becomes: "Have they not looked at the sky, how much We have deposited in its constellations and other things of beneficial and harmful signs, such as rains and thunderbolts?" He then linked to it what arises from that on the earth, in His saying, expressing wonder at them: ﴿Have they not looked at the earth?﴾

Since they were blind to contemplating that, He expressed the indication of it with the particle of limit (ila), saying: ﴿to the earth﴾, that is, in its vastness, the variety of its regions and its soils. He drew attention to the abundance of what He made of all kinds, saying: ﴿How many a pair have We caused to grow in it﴾, that is, by what We possess of greatness, ﴿in it﴾ after it had been dry and dead, with no vegetation in it, ﴿of every kind﴾, that is, a type resembling one another, so that no type fitting for them in this world was left except that We caused much of it to grow, ﴿noble﴾, that is, abundant in benefits, praiseworthy in outcomes, free of any baseness in it, from trees, crops and all other plants of varied colors in their blossoms and flowers, [and] their tastes and qualities, their benefits and their scents, and beyond that, matters whose limit no one encompasses and whose number no one counts except He who created them, all while they are watered with one water. "Noble" (karim) is a description of everything that is pleasing and praiseworthy in its category, and it is the opposite of "base" (la'im).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 8:

When that was dazzling to the intellect, constantly alerting it to the great power of its Maker and the wondrous quality of His choice, He connected to it His saying: ﴿Indeed in that is surely a sign﴾, that is, in that great matter of causing growth and in the admonitions that preceded it, despite their abundance, ﴿a sign﴾, that is, a very great indication ﴿for them﴾ of the complete power to resurrect and to other things, sufficient for calling to faith and restraining from transgression. Perhaps He made it singular ("a sign") despite their multiplicity to indicate that the indicators to Him are equal in their feet in pointing (to Him): the firmly grounded are satisfied by one, while others do not turn back for anything. ﴿And~ while~ the state is that it~ was not~ in the form in which We created them, ~most of them~ being~ believers﴾, that is, the human beings are not firmly rooted in faith, because ﴿most of them do not believe in God without associating others with Him﴾ [Yusuf: 106].

(p-12) "And indeed" — that is, and the case is that "your Lord" — that is, the One who blessed you with the sending (of the Messenger), who made the hearts of the pure (ones) yield to you, and who kept far from you the stubborn wretched ones — "is indeed" ﴿the Mighty﴾, that is, the One able over everyone whom He compels to faith and to exact retribution from them, and ﴿the Merciful﴾ in that He did not hasten to punish them, but sent down the Book to them out of gentleness toward them and as an explanation of what He is pleased with, so as to establish proof against those who are destined for humiliation, and to turn the hearts of those among them whom He singles out toward faith. Abu Hayyan said: the meaning is that He is Mighty in His vengeance upon the disbelievers, and Merciful to the believers of every nation — end of quote.

From here, may He be glorified and exalted, begins another illustration of the Criterion (al-Furqan) in showing power through seizing (the wrongdoers) at the time of vengeance, since the one who was called did not give thanks for the blessing by refusing to answer the call of the Messengers, and the caller, after the obedience (to the Messenger) [from] hardships, abandoned supplication to the one sent. He related the reports of the nations as they really were, such that none of the People of the Book who lived among them could deny any part of that. For this reason, the first thing He struck their ears with was their story concerning Pharaoh and Moses, peace be upon him. Thus it is certainly established that this Book is clear in its matter and lofty in its rank, is not soothsaying nor poetry, as He will confirm that at the display of the outcome at its end, but rather it is from the Lord of the worlds, upon the tongue of the Master of the Messengers. And it is established that most of creation, despite that, is destined for ruin, even though the proof has been established; and the path became clear, because threading the remembrance into their hearts is similar in tightness to the arrangement of the arrow in what is shot with it. And it is established that He, may He be glorified, gives them respite and bestows upon them that in which is the life of their religions through sending Messengers and sending down Books, and that in which is the life of their bodies through giving them all that they need, as a display of the attribute of mercy; (p-13) then He takes vengeance upon them after a long respite and their persistence in the intoxications of heedlessness, as a disclosure of the attribute of might. All of that is for consolation to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and for lightening (his burden), and to inform him that there is no deficiency in his clarification and no shortcoming on his part.

When the attribute of might (ʿIzza) required destruction, and the attribute of mercy (Raḥma) required respite, and the former was given precedence, and their habit was to put first what matters most to them, which for them was more important, its danger was feared; so He followed that with the reports of these nations, as an indication of both attributes together, as encouragement and warning, and as an indication that mercy preceded wrath. Even though He mentioned the attribute that is fitting for it first, He does not punish except after clarification and with long respite. He left out from the story of their father Ibrahim, peace be upon him, any mention of destruction, as an indication of good news of gentleness toward his descendants, the Arabs, in respite, just as He was gentle with them in sending down and sending messengers. Since this story also contains consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding what he suffers of harm and denial, and consolation through Musa and Ibrahim, peace be upon them both, is more complete, because of their closeness to him, their sharing in the migration, and their aim toward the Holy Land; and since Musa, peace be upon him, was specially given the Book, after which the Qur'an has no like, and the signs such that no one before him brought their like, and the comforting of his eye through the guidance of his people, and their preservation after him of the Book, and the governance of the renewing Prophets of his Shari'a, and their not being wiped out by punishment and vengeance at their own hands against all their enemies, and the opening of the lands of the disbelievers at their hands after him (ﷺ), and other things in which they resembled this Ummah, together with their neighbourhood to the Arabs, even in the abode of migration and the place of support, so that in their acknowledgment of what they hear of their reports there would be the greatest miracle and the most complete proof, He placed those two in front, as a foremost matter, for Musa, peace be upon them both, and the greeting and honour. If the intent is to calm what the last of those [verses] left of fear of being overtaken by punishment, considering the attribute of might, then the estimate is: remember the effect of Our mercy through the length of Our respite toward your people, who are at the utmost of disbelief and error in the days of ignorance, by Our all-encompassing mercy in sending you to them while you are the most noble of messengers, and the sending down of this Book, which is the greatest of books. And "remember" [is implied] before "when" (idh). On the estimate of consolation, the conjunction is with those [verses], because their purpose is alerting, so the estimate is: take the signs of the Book and remember when ﴿your Lord called﴾, i.e., the one who does good to you with every good that can be done in this abode. And on the estimate of warning, the estimate is: or did they not see when your Lord called, and they are counted as having seen it, because the Jews were in their lands and within close reach of them, so either they knew the story from what they had heard from them, or they were prepared for it because they could ask them. Then He mentioned the one called, saying: ﴿Musa﴾, and followed it with what the calling was for, saying, explaining, since the calling has the sense of saying: ﴿that you go to the people﴾, i.e., those who have strength, and what strength, ﴿the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., by placing their strength on the correct reasoning that leads to faith in a place not its own.

When it was as if it were said, "Which people?", he said, substituting (*badal*, apposition) to indicate that the two expressions have one meaning, because they are deeply rooted in wrongdoing, due to their wronging themselves through disbelief and otherwise, and the wrongdoing of the Children of Israel and other servants: ﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾.

When the purpose of the message was to frighten them of God, exalted is He, and to inform them of His majesty, He resumed His speech, informing them of this in the context of rebuke against them, declaring His great anger toward them, recording their wrongdoing against them, and marveling at their state in their great oppression in it. He also (indicated) that His respite for them has been long, while they increase only in insolence and persistence in destructive sins: ﴿Will they not fear (God)?﴾, i.e., piety would arise from them.

Since it is known that whoever brings people something that opposes their desires is not accepted, he informed [whoever longed to know his answer] that he responded with what calls for asking for help, because he knew the gravity of this situation, by saying, turning toward something like: O Lord, indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as abandoned...

﴿He said, "My Lord"﴾ i.e., O You who are gentle with me (p-16) ﴿indeed I fear that they will deny me﴾ i.e., so no effect will follow from my coming to them, and they will plot against me. So grant me acceptance and awe by which You guard me from whoever wants harm for me. It is permissible that by "akhaafu" (I fear) he means "a'lamu" (I know) or "azunnu" (I think), so that "an" is the light form (mukhaffafa, the lightened form of inna), and the two verbs are then conjoined to "yukadhdhibun" (they deny) in the reading of the majority (qira'at al-jumhur) with the raf' (nominative), together with the permissibility of conjoining them to "akhaafu". [So the estimate becomes]

"And my breast tightens, and my tongue is not released" — or he said: "I fear that they will deny me, and my breast tightens" at their denial, or my fear of their denial of me is an emotional reaction, as is the way of people of honour and those of lofty resolve, because of the sharpness and firmness of determination that was implanted in them when they find no way forward. And Ya'qub (Ya'qub, i.e., Yaʿqūb, one of the readers) put the two verbs in the subjunctive, coordinating them with ﴿يُكَذِّبُونِ﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 12], on the basis that "an" (أنْ) is a governing particle (nasibah).

﴿لِسانِي﴾ [i.e.]: in expressing what You send me to them with, because of the stammer in its original state due to the knot in it caused by that ember which stung him in childhood. So when denial occurs, or he fears it, and the heart constricts, the spirit withdraws into its inner part and the stammer increases; thus there becomes a need for a helper who strengthens the heart so that it assists in releasing the tongue at the time of the stammer, lest the call be disrupted.

﴿فَأرْسِلْ﴾ i.e.: so, as a consequence of that which he cited as an excuse for not hastening to go at the command, I ask You to send ﴿إلى هارُونَ﴾ my brother, so that he may be a messenger from You, (p-17) and so that he may be a support for me "in what" I have to carry out of the message, helping with whatever results from that. His request is not an excuse to evade obedience; and seeking help suffices as evidence of acceptance, not of evasion.

When he had mentioned what the message entails, he first alluded to his seeking to have it made clear, because that matters most. He then followed it with what results from mere confrontation with them, let alone facing them with what they dislike, and so he said: ﴿And they have a charge against me﴾, that is, for my killing a soul from among them. He said "charge" (dhanb), even though the one killed was not protected, calling it by what they claim it to be; and for this reason he qualified it with "against me" (lahum). Also, because what he had come to do involved a specific command from God Almighty, ﴿so I fear﴾ [because of that] ﴿that they will kill me﴾, that is, because of that, together with what I add to it of confronting them, so I will not be able to carry out the message. So if Aaron is with me, he will support me in conveying it. All of this is a seeking of clarification and a seeking to ward off trial, and a seeking of well-being; it is not a hesitation about acceptance, as has already been stated explicitly in Surat Ta-Ha.

When the soul was eager to know His answer regarding these weighty matters, He relieved its anxiety with His words, informing him that He had granted his request in everything he asked: ﴿He said﴾, speaking as one of complete power and all-encompassing knowledge, as is His attribute, glorified is He: (p-18) ﴿No!﴾, that is, desist from this speech. Nothing of what you fear will happen, neither killing nor anything else. It is as if, since denial stood against the truth supported by proofs that strengthen their bearer, expand his breast, and exalt his cause, it was counted as nothing. ﴿And We have granted your request concerning your brother﴾, ﴿So go, both of you﴾, that is, you and he, supporting one another, toward what I have commanded you, and aided, ﴿with Our signs﴾, which indicate your truthfulness, with all the greatness they possess by their being attributed to Us. Then He gave the reason for His assurance to him in His words: ﴿Indeed We﴾, with all the greatness We possess, ﴿are with you﴾, that is, present when you both arrive at them, among those who follow you from your people. Then He gave another piece of information in His words: ﴿listening﴾, that is, hearing, with all the greatness We possess in power and other attributes of perfection, to what you say to them and what they say to you, so We are not absent from you nor are you absent from Us. We therefore act with you in aid and support as one who is capable and present acts for his beloved who listens to him with all his effort. For this reason He expressed it by listening. Abu Hayyan said: Our teacher, the master Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, used to prefer that by the plural form [the dual] and the address is meant only Musa and Harun, because the word "ma'a" (with) distinguishes one who is a disbeliever, for it is not said that Allah is "ma'ahu" (with him) in such a case. And as for the plural being intended as the dual, Sibawayh took it as: "as if they both, for their nobility," before Allah the Exalted, He treated them in address as a plural, since it is permissible to treat a single person in this way because of his nobility and greatness. End of quotation. This is a precious statement, supported (p-19) by placing the adverbial phrase first. In that case their address would accord with the Speaker, glorified is He, magnifying Himself, because the context calls for majesty, and the majesty of the Messenger derives from the majesty of the One who sent him. Moreover, it is possible that this is an indication of good news about those who will follow them, as I have estimated, and it is possible that the companionship is for all, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but that He is their fourth﴾ [al-Mujadila: 7], and so on.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 16:

When He, glorified is He, negated that anything of what Musa (peace be upon him) feared would occur in this emphatic manner, and since the manifestation of that would be more evident and clear in a confrontation of heads, He stated it explicitly in His saying: ﴿So come﴾, meaning: as a consequence of that guarantee of protection and preservation, I say to you both: come,

﴿to Pharaoh﴾ himself, even though his kingdom is great and his armies are mighty,

﴿and say﴾, meaning: at the moment of your arrival to him and to those who are with him: ﴿Indeed, we are a messenger﴾. He used the singular, intending by it the genus, which is suitable for the two of them, indicating by the singular that they are, in their mutual support and agreement, like a single soul. There is no contradiction, for it was either said twice, each time in a different form, or once in a form that conveys duality and agreement together, so it was permissible to express it with either of them. He did not use the dual here because the context does not call for it, namely to draw attention to our Prophet ﷺ's request for support, unlike what preceded in Surat Taha.

﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, meaning: the One who is good to all creation and who manages their affairs.

Then he mentioned what he intended by the message delivered to him, and said, expressing it with the particle of explanation (ay), because the Messenger (rasul) contains within it the meaning of the message (risala), which comprises the statement: ﴿that send﴾, i.e., let go and release;

and he returned the pronoun to the meaning of "messenger" (rasul), saying: ﴿with us the Children of Israel﴾, i.e., our people whom you have oppressed by enslaving them, and you have no authority over them; we shall take them away to the Holy Land which God promised us through the tongues of the prophets among our fathers, upon them be prayer and peace.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 18:

Since it was known that the two of them had complied with what Allah commanded them, and they came to him and said to him what they had been commanded to say, the soul became eager for his reply to them. So He, exalted is He, said, turning to words like His saying in the one before it: ﴿And they say, "What is this messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 7] and ﴿They take you not except in ridicule﴾ [al-Furqan: 41], and the like, as consolation for this noble Prophet and as a confirmation of the meaning of His saying, exalted is He,

﴿No!﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 15] and ﴿[We are] with you, listening﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 15], that Pharaoh, though he exaggerated in threats and intimidation, nothing from him frightens Musa, peace be upon him. ﴿He said﴾, that is, Pharaoh, when they had conveyed the message to him, addressing Musa, peace be upon him, knowing that he was the principal in it, and that his brother was merely a deputy, disapproving of his confronting him with such a thing and reproaching him, so that he would restrain his boldness by correcting such speech toward him: ﴿Did we not raise you﴾, that is, by our greatness which you witnessed,

﴿among us as a child﴾, that is, a young child recently born,

﴿and you remained among us﴾, that is, not among others, considering your attachment to us and your honor outwardly through us, ﴿for years of your life﴾, that is, many. So we have a right over you on account of that which should prevent you from confronting us with such a thing. It seems he expressed with what conveys hardship, as a metaphor for the period of his stay with him, that it was hardship for him, because he fell into what he feared, and he lost what he was guarding against by slaying the infants.

Then, when he reminded him of a favor that would move him to shame before Him, he reminded him of a sin deserving that he fear its consequence. So he said, overawing him by way of allusion to it: ﴿And you did your deed﴾, that is, the killing of the Copt. Then he emphasized his attribution to that, indicating that He had treated him with forbearance in order to shame him, so he said: ﴿which you did, and you were﴾, that is, while the situation was that you were ﴿among the disbelievers﴾, that is, ungrateful for My blessing and the right of My upbringing by killing those who are attributed to Me; or [it means] counting you among them because of your silence about them at that time, since before the prophethood he had not been commanded regarding them with anything, so he was being courteous toward them. It is as if he said: "And you were one of us, so why now do you disapprove of us and attribute disbelief to us?"

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 20:

﴿Qāla﴾ (He said), answering him in a scattered, disordered manner, trusting in God's promise of safety, acknowledging what he had been muttering about regarding killing, because he had not been certain of it, and he did not abandon killing him except in seeking clarity (bayyinah): ﴿Fa'altuhā idhan﴾ (I did it then), i.e., when I killed him,

﴿Wa-anā mina al-ḍāllīn﴾ (and I was among those who went astray). [I.e.:] I did not know the religion. So I was standing aside from every direction until my Lord guides me to what He wills. Ibn Jarir said: "The Arabs place ḍalāl (straying) in the place of jahl (ignorance), and jahl in the place of ḍalāl," — end of quotation. And previously, in [the commentary on] al-Fatihah, al-Hirali made a precious statement on this, [to the effect] that this deed was from me a mistake.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 21:

﴿Then I fled from you﴾ means: as a consequence of that act and its aftermath, I fled ﴿from you﴾, that is, from you (Pharaoh) because of your might [and from your people, because they incited you against me] ﴿when I feared you﴾ [for my own life, that you would kill me on account of that victim whom I had killed by mistake, although he was an unbeliever whose blood was forfeit] ﴿Then my Lord granted me﴾ [He who had shown me kindness by raising me among you, under the protection of my mother, safe from the wrongdoing you had devised out of fear of me] ﴿wisdom﴾, that is, knowledge by which I act as wise judges act, ﴿and made me one of the messengers﴾. That is: strive now with all your effort, for I do not fear you, neither for killing nor for anything else.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 22:

When Pharaoh's speech combined both a reminder of favor and a rebuke, he began with his answer to the rebuke, since it was the more recent and therefore closer [in mention], and because it was more important. Then he followed it with his answer concerning the favor he had been reminded of. He said, rebuking him, reproaching him, and denouncing him, but he omitted the particle of denial, for conciseness in speech and courtesy in address: ﴿And is it a favor of which you remind me﴾, that is, this upbringing [the hideous thing, monstrous in its ugliness] which you mention to me,

﴿a favor you count against me?﴾ (p. 23) Since its cause was his oppression of his people, he made the favor itself the thing to be described, and said, substituting for it [as an alert to its nullification, and an announcement that it, by being a calamity, is more deserving than the favor it is counted as]: ﴿That you have enslaved﴾ [that is, your enslaving and subjugating them in that unprecedented and reprehensible manner] my people ﴿the Children of Israel﴾, that is, you made them slaves through injustice and aggression, though they are the descendants of prophets, and of their forefather Joseph, peace be upon him. ﴿Upon you﴾ is the favor—by preserving your lives first, and freeing your necks second—which you could never repay at all. Then that did not suffice you, until you did what no enslaver would do: you ordered the killing of their sons. So that was the cause of my being delivered to you, so that I might be saved from your injustice, as its explanation has passed and will come [God willing] in full in Surat al-Qasas.

When the noble Kalim (Moses, the one who spoke with Allah), peace be upon him, addressed the vile, despicable one (Pharaoh), hoping that he would restrain him from confronting him with what he disliked and would bring him back to conciliation, Pharaoh did not do so. Moses understood that in this final reply there was disparagement of him and an attempt to render him powerless, as well as an affirmation of Allah's complete power and all-encompassing knowledge in what He had arranged concerning Moses, peace be upon him. He understood also that Pharaoh could not stand up to that with a reply, and no credit would come to him from any statement he made in it. So Pharaoh turned away from it, to answering him about the Messenger, with what would also confuse his people, lest they turn away from him. Allah, exalted is He, informed about this exchange of theirs with His words, in the manner of a reply to someone who seems to have asked: "What did he say to him in response to these words, which were like arrows?" :

﴿Pharaoh said﴾, evading the answer of Moses, peace be upon him, because it contained rebuke and rendering him powerless, denying his Creator in a manner of feigned ignorance, just as these people denied the Most Merciful while feigning ignorance, though they are the most knowing of people about most of His acts. Pharaoh was as aware of the statement of Moses, peace be upon him: "You know well that none has sent down these but the Lord of the heavens and the earth" , as one would expect. So he said:

﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ That is: the One whom you claim you are His messenger. He asked with "what" about His reality, while in fact he intended only to deny Him.

[Since defining His essence (exalted is He) by itself is impossible, because He is not composite, defining Him can only be done through external, necessary, manifest signs, the listener became eager to know the answer to it, so He resumed His speech informing about him]: ﴿He said﴾, that is, Moses, [turning away from defining Him by anything other than His acts, to make known that He has no likeness, and that His existence is distinct from the existence of everything other than Him], [defining Him (exalted is He) by His most evident acts, which no one can claim to share in], [alluding to their request for the quiddity (al-mahiyyah, the whatness or essence of a thing) by saying that He has no equal]: I say to you, and to whomever you intend by seeking the reality, to deceive them: He is ﴿the Lord﴾ [that is, the Creator, Originator and Manager of] ﴿the heavens﴾ [all of them] ﴿and the earth﴾ [even if their bodies are far apart from one another] ﴿and what is between them﴾. That manifests the world, which is His making, and you are not independent of it for the blink of an eye. So this is the favour, not your favour upon me by raising me [until] I became independent of you. This is the reproach for goodness together with disobedience through ingratitude, not your reproach of my people by destroying them while they are in your obedience, and their predecessors have a favour upon you that you do not ignore. ﴿If you are﴾ [that is, a firm state] ﴿certain﴾, that is, characterised by what the people of knowledge of the principles of religion (usul al-din) are characterised by, of confidence in what you believe [a stable characterisation]. The answer: you know that, and you know that there is no more decisive answer than it, because what is mentioned is changing, so for it there is a Changer who does not change, and He is this One whom We sent, that is, if you have certainty, then you know Him, due to the intensity of His manifestation and the universality of His light.

(p-25)

Pharaoh said to those around him, [the eminent men of his people], still deceiving: "Do you not listen?" That is, do you not give ear to him with all your effort? This is a statement whose outward sense is that he warned them against denial, for he asked about the essence (of the Lord of the worlds), and was answered with something other than it. It could bear another meaning if pressed upon, so it is of his subtle deception.

He said: "Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones."

When he had rebuked the accursed one in his answer, and it was likely that he claimed the two horizons and what lies between them of space were uncreated, so the listener longed for a reply that would bind him, [al-Biqa'i] took up anew the cure for the feebleness of this question by saying: ﴿He said﴾, i.e., Moses, specifying after generalizing [with something that cannot be disputed, because the existence of its instances is observed after they had not existed]: ﴿Your Lord﴾, i.e., the One who brings you into being, nurtures you, and bestows favour upon you, ﴿and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones.﴾ (p-26) And Pharaoh, whom you acknowledge as your lord, was at that time pure nothingness, or mere water in his father's loins. Thus it is refuted that any of them could be a lord to those who came after him, just as it is refuted that any of those destroyed before them could be a lord to them, because all of them are nothing.

Then, when he had made clear by this the falsehood of what had led them to believe in his lordship, he could not restrain himself and said, ﴿Indeed, your messenger﴾ sarcastically, indicating that the messenger should be the most intelligent of people. Then he increased the matter in clarity by his saying: ﴿who has been sent to you﴾, meaning: while you are the most intelligent of people,

﴿is surely a madman﴾, since he does not understand that I am asking him about the reality of the one who sent him. How then is he fit to be a messenger from the kings?

When Pharaoh showed bad manners, and the listener's eagerness to know the answer to his question grew intense, God, exalted is He, resumed the report and related that Moses mentioned to him something he could not claim as obedience to himself, [and it is far more variable and more wondrous in its transformations], by saying: ﴿Lord of the East and the West﴾, meaning the risings and the settings, their times and their places, ﴿and what is between them﴾, meaning the people who are not under your obedience, and the animals and inanimate things, by reason of what you see of His power in turning the luminous bodies: the rising of the sun, the moon and the stars, and their setting, [and what appears from them of night and day], in various alternations and close successive movements, (p-27) which, were they not so, you would not know anything of your affairs, nor be able to manage your conditions. This proof is the clearest of all, because of the repetition of motion in it and other of its signs. For this reason Nimrod was confounded when Abraham, peace be upon him, cast it at him.

And when [he (ﷺ) called him gently], and Pharaoh had shown bad manners toward him in his earlier answer, he concluded this proof with his words: ﴿If you are people who understand﴾, meaning: then you know this. So he gave them the choice between acknowledging madness or reason, by what he pointed to of the proofs, in response to their attributing madness to him, through their silence and the saying of their great one without any doubt, as a refutation of them from error and a rescue from manifest ignorance. [So his statement was more cutting, though it was gentler, and more manifest, though it was more concealed and more noble.]

When he (Pharaoh) knew that Moses had cut him off by the clarity of what he had made manifest, and he matched him in harshness to the point that if he kept silent about it, it would weaken his position and dampen the resolve of his men, [he spoke with what silence would have been better than, so God Most High informed by His saying]: ﴿He said﴾, turning away from argument after having plunged into it to mere overpowering, which is the clearest sign of being at a loss: ﴿If you take a god other than me﴾, i.e., you deliberately took him, [and you singled him out by directing all your intent toward him], ﴿I will surely make you among those imprisoned﴾, i.e., one of those who are in my prisons, as you know [of my state in my power, and of (p-28) my prisons in their dreadfulness, and of the state of those in them from the severity of confinement and the harshness of restraint].

﴿He said﴾ responding in the manner that is best, loosening the reins so that the desire for clarification is served, so that no excuse remains for any human being, in hope that he will desist from tyranny and return to faith. [For it is a customary practice that people incline to fairness and return to truth and acknowledgment.] ﴿Even if﴾, i.e., "Will you imprison me even if" ﴿I bring you something clear﴾, i.e., for my message.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 31:

﴿Qāla﴾ (He said), hoping to find a pretext for denial or confusion: ﴿Then bring it﴾, meaning: as a consequence of your saying this, I say to you: bring that thing ﴿if you are﴾ [meaning: being one who is firmly established in it] ﴿of the truthful﴾ [meaning: in what you claim of messengership and a clear sign].

This is an indication that, by his earlier speech, he had come to be regarded by him as not among their number. [It follows from this that a miracle is brought only by one who is truthful, because it is a confirmation from God of the one who makes the claim, and the custom of Him, glorified and exalted, runs such that He does not confirm the liar.]

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 32:**

﴿Then he cast﴾, i.e., this resulted from that and immediately followed it: he cast down.

[Since the speech was directed] to Musa, peace be upon him, [and his pronoun was unambiguous, he did not state his name, relying on the pronoun, so he said]: ﴿his staff﴾, i.e., the one whose signs Allah the Exalted had shown him, as was mentioned in more than one surah. ﴿And behold, it was a serpent﴾, i.e., a snake of extreme size, ﴿plainly visible﴾, i.e., clearly a serpent, with no doubt in the mind of the one who saw it, unlike what happens with matters of magic [of imaginings and illusions].

(p-29) ﴿And he drew out his hand﴾, i.e., the hand which had been burned when he took the live coal while he was in the lap of Pharaoh. Pharaoh had exerted his utmost effort to treat it, with every physician he could muster, but he was unable to heal it. He drew it out of his collar after he had shown Pharaoh it in the state Pharaoh was accustomed to seeing it, then he put it back into his collar. ﴿Then behold, it﴾ after the drawing out ﴿was white to the beholders﴾, i.e., a whiteness that strongly prompts people to gaze at it, because it departs from the customary, having a light like the light of the sun that nearly dazzles the eyes.

Said Pharaoh to the chiefs around him, when the matter had become clear to him, deceiving their minds out of fear of their believing: ﴿Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer.﴾ That is, one of great knowledge of sorcery. He specifically attributed this statement to him in this surah because the whole context is about his singling out the address to what preceded, and in view of ﴿Then their necks will remain humbled before it﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 4], because his humbling is the humbling of those beneath him, so the indication of it is more apparent. This does not preclude that his people said it, displaying obedience, as has passed in al-A'raf.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 35:

When he (Pharaoh) had made them stand still by what he had imagined for them, he incited them to protect themselves. Then, casting off the cloak of pride because of what the power of the miracle had overcome him with, he said: ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land﴾, that is, this land which is your support, ﴿with his magic﴾, that is, because of what he has brought of it, for it necessitates that people follow him, so that he is able to do what he wishes [to them]. Then he said to his people, those whom he used to claim were his slaves and that he was their god, something that indicated that his strength had failed. (p-30) He let down from his shoulders the greatness of lordship, and his muscles trembled, so that he made himself one who is commanded, after having claimed to be one who commands, indeed a powerful god. He said: ﴿So what do you advise?﴾, that is, in repelling him from what he wants to do to us.

"They said": that is, the chiefs (al-Mala') who had been conspiring against him before the Hijra, intending to kill him: ﴿Put him off﴾, that is, delay him, ﴿and his brother﴾. They did not order his killing or anything close to it. So glory be to the One who casts the Spirit by His command upon whomever He wills of His servants: everything fears him, while he fears none but his Creator. ﴿And send heralds to the cities who will gather [all the magicians]﴾, that is, men who will gather the sorcerers. The origin of hashr (gathering) is to assemble, and to do so early in the day (bukrah).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 37:

﴿Yatūka﴾ (they will bring you). It seems they understood the intensity of his anxiety, so they calmed him by using the particle of comprehensiveness and the intensive form, and they said: ﴿every sorcerer﴾, meaning one eloquent in magic, ﴿well-versed﴾, meaning one who has reached the utmost in knowledge of it after having reached the utmost in practice. He used the passive form to indicate the greatness of his kingdom, and so he said:

Then the sorcerers were gathered (﴿فَجُمِعَ﴾), that is, by the easiest of matters given the great standing he had among them, ﴿the sorcerers﴾, as has been mentioned more than once, ﴿for the appointed time of a known day﴾, at its time and place, which was the forenoon of the Day of Adornment (Yawm al-Zinah), as passed in Surat Taha. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, that it coincided with Saturday, the first day of their year, and it was the day of Nayruz (Nayrūz, the Persian New Year).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 39:

﴿And it was said﴾, i.e., by the word of one who is accepted, because he is from Pharaoh, ﴿to the people﴾, i.e., all of them, urging them to hasten to gather at Pharaoh's command, and testing them to see whether they had turned away from his religion, knowing that the manifest miracle, among which is his inability to inflict any kind of harm on whoever confronts him with anything that gives no hope of being confronted even with its lesser part, has left no doubt that he is a subjugated, overpowered servant, and that this obliges following Moses, peace be upon him. ﴿Will you gather?﴾, i.e., [a gathering in which you are firmly established, for it is in the hearts just as it is in the bodies], all of you, so that it may be more awe-inspiring for you. [This speaker made it appear attractive to them to remain upon the falsehood they were on by mentioning the side of the magicians, even though he had stipulated victory for it, and he did not permit mention of the side of Moses, peace be upon him, so he said]

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 40:

﴿Perhaps we will follow the magicians﴾ Because whoever obeys the command of the king, his state is that of one from whom following his party is hoped for. ﴿If it is they who are﴾ [i.e., exclusively] ﴿the victorious﴾. That is: [a victory about which there is no doubt that it arises from power] and we shall turn away from the command of Musa, concerning which the king disputed, [and this is actually what they intended; he expressed it this way as a metonymy for it, because it is more indicative of the king's greatness], and he expressed it with the particle of doubt to show fairness and to win over the people, along with their certainty of the magicians' triumph, because of what had become firmly rooted in their minds over long periods of error, which Iblis is never heedless of adorning, although changing what is familiar is extremely difficult. And he said.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 41:

﴿Fa-lammā﴾ with the fa' (fa') indicating the swiftness of their gathering, as a sign of the vastness of his dominion and the abundance of his greatness. ﴿Jā'a al-saḥaratu﴾, that is, those who were in all the lands of Egypt,

﴿qālū li-Fir'awna﴾ stipulating a reward while there was need for the deed, so that this would be more fitting for a good promise and the success of the aim. ﴿A-inna lanā la-ajran﴾ (p-32) and they put it in the form of a question out of courtesy toward him. They said: ﴿in kunnā﴾, that is, supposing that we are firmly established in it, ﴿naḥnu﴾ specifically ﴿al-ghālibīn﴾ (the victors), using the particle of doubt together with their certainty of victory, to frighten him that if he does not do well by their promise, they will not give him sincere counsel.

Then it was said, in answer to whoever might seem to have asked about his reply: ﴿He said﴾, responding to what they asked for: ﴿Yes﴾, meaning, you will have that. He added to it something better than wealth in the eyes of the people of this world, emphasizing it by saying: ﴿And indeed you will then be among those brought near﴾, meaning, near to me, if you prevail. He added "إذًا" (idhan, "then") here as further emphasis, because of what that implies of distancing him from faith through the clarity of the proof. This was to ease matters for the one addressed with all of this (ﷺ), and to console him, so that he would not burden himself over those he called to faith not becoming believers. What follows, namely the sorcerers' swift embrace of faith after they had sworn by His might with the utmost emphasis, confirms the verse: ﴿So their necks remained bowed before them﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 4].

Once the listener was eager for the response of Allah's Prophet Musa (peace be upon him), it was answered with His words: ﴿Musa said to them﴾ (peace be upon him), meaning: intending to nullify their sorcery, since it can only be accomplished through their casting it, not merely by their casting it, while being unconcerned with them in their multitude or their knowledge, after they had given him the choice, as in other than this surah: ﴿Throw down what you are going to throw down﴾, whatever it may be, belittling it in comparison with the command of Allah.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 44:

﴿So they cast﴾ means: as a consequence of Musa's (peace be upon him) words and his challenge, they cast ﴿their ropes and their staves﴾, which they had prepared for sorcery, ﴿and said﴾, swearing, (p-٣٣) ﴿by the might of Pharaoh﴾, emphasizing with every kind of emphasis, ﴿Indeed, we are the victors﴾, meaning exclusively, without any exception. It was the saying of one confident in himself, resolved not to leave any branch of sorcery that he knew without bringing it forth. Thus, whoever swears by other than Allah, such as saying: "By the life of so-and-so, and by the head of so-and-so," and the like, then he is following this jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance).

Since the pronoun referring to the name of Musa (peace be upon him) was used first in the initial casting, because the discourse was with him, there was no ambiguity as to who was the agent, and because the discourse here concerns the magicians, and they concluded with the mention of Pharaoh and his might, he explicitly named Musa (peace and blessings be upon him) to remove any confusion, saying: ﴿So Musa cast down﴾, meaning: as a consequence of the magicians' act and its following, Musa cast down ﴿his staff﴾, and he contrasted the plural of what they had cast with the singular of what Musa cast, because it is more indicative of the miracle. He said: ﴿his staff﴾, meaning: the one We had made a sign for him. As a consequence of his casting, there is His saying: ﴿and behold, it swallowed up﴾, meaning: it immediately devoured swiftly and voraciously ﴿what they were falsely showing﴾, meaning: they were turning it away from its true face and reality, which is being inanimate, through their tricks and their imaginings, so that it was thought to be snakes slithering.

Fa-ulqiya (﴿فَأُلْقِيَ﴾): that is, immediately after their act, without any delay. ﴿The sorcerers were made to fall down prostrate﴾ [that is, they prostrated with tremendous speed], to the point that it was as if someone had thrown them down [against their will] because of the strength of their haste, since they knew that this was from Allah. Thus they became pious and righteous in the evening, after they had come in the morning of that day as sorcerers.

Since it is as if it were said: "This was their deed, so what was their statement?" It is said: (p-34) ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds"﴾, meaning: the One to whom Moses, peace be upon him, called, or whatever he spoke of.

Then they specified him, to remove Pharaoh's confusion, by what admits of no other reading. They said, as a clarification: ﴿Lord﴾. No summons called for departing here from the original (wording), so he said, as an expression of their speech: ﴿of Moses and Aaron﴾, meaning: the two who did us good by alerting us to Him and guiding us to Him, and by the truth of the two of them, through what He caused to occur at their hands.

When Pharaoh feared that the people would follow them (the magicians), because of what they saw that had alarmed them about their affair, and it had already been mentioned what makes known that the one who denounced them was Pharaoh himself, God, exalted is He, said, reporting about him: ﴿He said﴾, without mentioning the agent, namely Pharaoh, because there is no ambiguity. [The aim of the surah does not require explicitness, as in al-A'raf, but rather suits turning away from him and relieving oneself of him], denouncing, hastening, and creating the impression that he only punishes for hastening without permission, not for the act itself, and that his purpose was only to make sure, so that by this imagining he might delay the people from hastening to faith until some time. ﴿Have you believed in him﴾, that is, in Musa, peace be upon him. He singled him out with the pronoun because he is the principal figure in this mission. The real meaning of the speech is: "You have bestowed assent upon what he reported from God on his account, magnifying him thereby," ﴿before I give you permission﴾, that is, to believe. Then he gave a reason for their act that implies it came from deceit and trickery, not from good following, so he said: ﴿Indeed, he﴾, that is, (p-35) Musa, peace be upon him, ﴿is your chief﴾.

Since this indicates attributing to him the practice of sorcery, and that he knows it better than they do, which is why he overpowered them, he clarified it with his words: ﴿who taught you magic﴾, so that you agreed with him upon this act, in order to strip the kingdom from its owners. This is what everyone who hears it knows to be a lie with certainty, for Musa, peace be upon him, was raised only in his own household and remained so until he fled from them to Madyan. He did not know magic, nor did he meet a magician, nor did he travel except to Madyan, and then he returned only as one calling to God. But falsehood predominates in the land of Egypt, and its people are the swiftest of things to listen to it and to submit to it.

When he had held the listeners in suspense by what he had imagined for them of this falsehood, whose falsity is evident to every person of insight, he emphasized the prohibition with a threat, so he said: ﴿But you will soon know﴾, that is, what I will do to you. That is, as a consequence of what you have done, I will punish you with a certain, great punishment. He used the particle of deferment (ḥarf al-tanfīs, the particle sawfa), fearing that he might not be able to overpower them, so that everyone would know his incapacity and would believe. Together with what it contains, in reality, of emphasis in the threat upon the magicians, which did not affect them, in comparison with the sign that God had shown them, which established them in a state of submission. Then he explained what he had left vague with his words: ﴿I will surely cut off﴾, in the form of the verb (ṣīghat al-tafʿīl, the intensive form), because of the multiplicity of the cutting and of those cut off, ﴿your hands and your feet﴾. [Then] he explained the manner of their cutting, so he said: ﴿on opposite sides﴾. He increased the terror further, so he said: ﴿and I will surely crucify you all﴾.

(p. 36) Then the Exalted One resumed relating their answer, saying: ﴿They said﴾.

[Since it had already been mentioned here that they ascribed to him a might that necessitates greater fear of him, their saying] ﴿No harm﴾ [was fitting]. That is, there is no harm at all upon us by which he could gain power over us [regarding what you threaten us with. Rather, for us, in patience under it, if it befalls us, there is the greatest reward from God. And there came] the all-encompassing negation in this surah, as a declaration that Pharaoh would not be able to harm them. This confirms what was indicated at the beginning of the narrative by ﴿kalla﴾ ("كلا", "by no means") and by ﴿mustami'un﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 15] (listening). For the pursuit by the followers of Musa, peace be upon him, would harm him and constrict his breast. And from the explicit wording of the narratives, in His saying: ﴿You two and those who follow you will be the victors﴾ [al-Qasas: 35]. [Then] they gave the reason for that by their saying: ﴿Indeed we﴾, that is, by your doing that to us, if God empowers you over us, ﴿to our Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to us alone, ﴿will be returning﴾, that is, death is inevitable for us. So let us be content with what our Lord has decreed for us of states. Your judgment is only over this body for an hour of a day, and then there is no judgment over the soul except by God, who is worthy of rewarding us for that with the bliss of eternity. This is the meaning of their saying, giving the reason for what preceded it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 51:

﴿Indeed, we hope that our Lord will forgive us our sins﴾ — i.e., will cover them with a thorough covering — ﴿our Lord, who has been good to us by guiding us﴾ — ﴿our sins﴾, i.e., those which we committed in advance, despite their great number. Then they gave a reason for their hope despite the abundance of their sins by saying: ﴿that we were﴾, i.e., a state that is for us like an innate nature,

﴿the first of the believers﴾, i.e., among the people of this station. They expressed it with hope to indicate that all the causes of felicity come from Him, the Exalted, so that it is as if there were no cause from them at all. (p-37)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 52:

When He, glory be to Him, related of the state of the call what sufficed as consolation for whoever intended these two Prophets with harm and mockery regarding those to whom they called, and made them the superiors, [and] their weakness and paucity did not harm them, nor did their enemy's strength and abundance benefit him, He began to console [the Prophet] with what He had brought about during the journey, saying, leaving out what remains of it because this was mentioned in it, and linking it to this narrative: ﴿And We inspired﴾, i.e., by the majesty We possess when We wished to decide the matter and fulfil the promise, ﴿to Moses: Travel by night﴾, i.e., go by night, while Pharaoh and his hosts were occupied with the death of their firstborn and preparing them ﴿with My servants﴾, i.e., the Children of Israel [whom You honoured], accompanying them toward the direction of the Sea of al-Qulzum, paying no heed to Pharaoh and not disturbed by him; and take with you meat and unleavened bread for haste, and smear your thresholds with blood, for I had instructed the angels who slay the firstborn not to enter a house whose door bears blood. Then He gave the reason for His command to him to travel at night with His words: ﴿Indeed you will be pursued﴾, i.e., do not think that because of the multitude of signs they have seen they will cease to pursue you; so hasten to depart, so that you may get far from them to the place where I had decreed from eternity that My glory would appear, and the intent is that they would meet them at the sea. [And] he did not conceal their pursuit from Moses, peace be upon him, because he was not affected by it, since he was certain of the protection of the noble promise, given with that emphasis.

Since the sense was: "So move with My servants by night" in compliance with the command, after the middle of the night, he followed it with His saying: ﴿Then Pharaoh sent heralds into the cities﴾, that is, when morning came and he was informed about them, ﴿gathering [troops]﴾, that is, men who would gather the soldiers with force and might, even if they were unwilling, and who would say (this) to strengthen their hearts and stir up their resolve.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 54:

﴿Indeed, these﴾ is a demonstrative with the particle of proximity, to belittle them, indicating that they are within the grasp (of Allah) even though they are far away, because of their weakness and the strength of the people of Pharaoh; so they are not in a position to be feared for their power or their resistance,

﴿are indeed a small band﴾, i.e., a group and a fragment of people.

Since their paucity is only in relation to the multitude and strength of the people of Pharaoh, and the awe of enslavement they hold over them, and since the expression "shirdhima" (a small band) could give the impression that they were in the extreme of scarcity, (the author) removed this illusion by using the plural rather than the singular, to convey that it is one statement after another, not a description; and that the expression "shirdhima" is only to indicate the scattering of hearts. The plural, especially the sound masculine plural (lil-salama), while also indicating paucity, is more indicative that they are scattered groups. There is also in it an indication that they, despite their weakness through small numbers, are hopeless of being aided by reinforcement, and they have no preparation for fighting due to lack of equipment, (p-39) because they were never among those who fight, just as you say of someone you despise: "He is too low to do such and such." So He said: ﴿they are few﴾, i.e., in relation to the countless hosts we possess, even if they are themselves numerous; so there is no multitude for them that could prevent you, O gathered ones, from following them. Al-Baghawi said, on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: they were six hundred thousand and ninety thousand, and the number of the companions of Pharaoh cannot be counted. End of quote.

All of this is an explanation that Pharaoh, despite the extreme magnitude of his greatness, was not able to reach the slightest effect against Musa, peace be upon him, nor those who followed him, in fulfilment of the promise mentioned earlier at the beginning of the story.

When al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) had mentioned what would prevent fear from following them, he mentioned what necessitates urging against them and warns against lagging in it, so he said: ﴿Indeed, they are enraging us﴾, while we are in what we are of multitude and greatness, ﴿enraging us﴾. That is: by what they have caused us grief with of themselves, and what they borrowed of adornment, from vessels of gold and silver and precious garments; so there should be no mercy in your hearts protecting them.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 56:**

Since the root *sh-r-dh-m* (شَرْذَمَ) revolves around the idea of being cut off and separated, its use here indicates that they, despite being few, are scattered and not of one heart. He mentioned that (p-٤٠) following them is the cure for the disease of hesitation, so he followed it with what removes from the one who holds back his excuses, and said: ﴿And indeed we are a united host﴾. That is: I and you are one group, gathered under the authority of the king, with one heart.

When he had indicated with this report the opposite of what the Children of Israel were in, despite their small number, which is itself a cause of boldness against them, he gave a second report that increases boldness against them, in contrast to what was indicated by "few" (قَلِيلُونَ) of weakness. So he said: ﴿always on guard﴾. That is: and we, even with the unity of our hearts, our nature and disposition is caution. We are never without readiness for battle and for facing the brave. Nothing prevents us from it, neither travel nor anything else. As for my part, it is by pouring wealth upon you and bestowing provisions among you, and placing things in their proper places in regard to land and men. As for your part, it is by using trustworthiness in obedience to the king, in placing everything he gives you in its proper place, such as preparing weapons, ships, provisions, and everything the warrior needs. In addition, you have the honor and strength, the lofty pride and great self-esteem, together with boldness, courage, and steadfastness in confronting realities, guarded by reason and surrounded by resolve that prevents adversaries from daring against you or plotting against you.

It is related that he [a certain ruler] managed the land tax of Egypt by dividing it into four parts: one for his ministers, scribes, and soldiers; (p-٤١) the second for digging canals and building dikes; the third for himself and his children; and the fourth was distributed among the districts (kuwar). If they suffered thirst, drought, or the ruin of a crop, or the death of workers, he would strengthen them with it. It is also narrated that a people came to him and said: "We need to dig a canal to restore our lands," so he gave permission for this and appointed an official over them. The official collected a great amount of the land tax of that region into the public treasury (bayt al-mal). He then asked how much they had spent on their canal, and it was one hundred thousand dinars. So he ordered that it be brought to them, but they refused to accept it. He said: "Throw it upon them, for when a king grows rich from the wealth of his subjects, he becomes poor and they become poor; and when the subjects grow rich from the wealth of their king, he and they become rich."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 57:

Since the implied sense is: they obeyed his command and went forth from every difficult and easy place, he (Allah) follows this with His statement, informing them of the outcome of their affair: ﴿So We expelled them﴾ [i.e.] by the power We possess, a swift expulsion from that which no one would willingly leave ﴿from gardens﴾ i.e., orchards that deserve to be called such ﴿and springs﴾ with which there is no need for the Nile or rain.

"And treasures" of wealth, known by the measure of the bounty they possess that is surplus to them, [together with] the complete readiness they have for such a purpose. "And a noble station" of dwellings [i.e., in a form that pleases the one who sees it], because it is at the utmost of beauty, so that one does not say of it: "Would that it were such-and-such," or "It were such-and-such."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 26, verse 59:

Since such an exit is something to be deemed strange, he pointed to the greatness of the power over it by saying: ﴿Thus﴾, meaning: like that wondrous removal which Pharaoh intended for his people, in its swiftness and the perfection of its awe, We removed them, by making it easy for him and for them, and by providing them with the means, in accordance with what Our wisdom required. Or (it means) like that exit which We have related to you, We removed them; that is, what actually occurred of their departure corresponded to what We expressed about it, or the matter which We have related in its entirety, as We said [and] its first is the most firmly established, the best and the most excellent. ﴿And We caused to inherit it﴾, meaning: those blessings hidden (from view) merely by their departure in potential and by their destruction in actuality, ﴿the Children of Israel﴾, meaning: We made them such that they would inherit them, because We had left them no barrier preventing them from them after they had been held in contempt under the hands of their owners. As for their inheritance of them in actuality, there is an issue with it, owing to His saying in al-Dukhan: ﴿another people﴾ [al-Dukhan: 28].

Then, having described the departure, He described its consequence, saying, arranging it upon it by the act and upon the inheriting by potential: ﴿So they pursued them﴾, that is, they made themselves followers of them, ﴿at sunrise﴾, that is, they entered upon the time of the sun's rising, meaning its appearance at dawn of the night in the middle of which the Children of Israel had traveled. Had it not been for the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing, breaking that custom, it would not have been within the usual course of things in less than ten days, for it is a matter that kings are incapable of achieving like it. How swift that gathering is! And how vast that equipment is!
